source: FAO/OIE/World Bank, "Good Practices for Biosecurity in the Pig Sector - Issues and Options in Developing and Transition Countries", FAO Animal Production and Health Paper No. 169, Rome, 2010.
text: For free-range/scavenging pigs - the most common system for smallholders and the hardest to protect because pigs roam and cannot be fully controlled - a small set of low-cost measures still meaningfully reduces disease risk: treat the whole village as the unit that needs protecting, since village pigs usually mix freely and share health status; any new pig brought into the village, especially one bought at a market, should be quarantined and observed for at least 30 days before mixing with other pigs; never sell or slaughter a visibly sick pig for meat, even though this is a common practice when farmers fear losing the animal entirely - selling sick pigs at a market spreads disease to many other farms at once; never feed pigs raw, unboiled food scraps or restaurant/kitchen waste - if scraps are used, they must be boiled for at least one hour at 100°C first; report unusual pig deaths to local animal health services rather than quietly disposing of the carcass, and bury or burn dead pigs rather than dumping them; and clean (and disinfect if possible) the night shelter where pigs are penned, since even scavenging pigs are usually housed at night for protection from theft and predators.
